title: International Fuel Cards for European Fleets in 2026
summary: How to choose an international fuel card for European fleets: acceptance, VAT recovery, tolls, EV charging, invoicing and credit terms.
body_markdown:
An international fuel card is no longer a niche product for long-haul hauliers. As more vans, service vehicles and electric fleets cross borders inside the EU, fleet managers and finance leads run into the same wall: domestic fuel cards stop working at the first foreign forecourt, VAT recovery is a paper-driven mess, and EV charging adds another layer of fragmentation. This guide sets out the criteria to judge any international fuel card on in 2026, so you can score a shortlist on your own routes instead of on brochures.


If you are also evaluating UK-only providers, see our[UK fuel-card comparison](https://www.getrally.com/blog/best-fuel-card-uk-2026) . If you run a smaller team, our companion guide to[small-business fuel cards](https://www.getrally.com/blog/best-fuel-card-for-small-business) is the better starting point.


## What an International Fuel Card Actually Means


An international fuel card is a fleet payment card that works across multiple countries rather than a single domestic network. Three things distinguish it from a domestic card.


First, **cross-border acceptance** . The card is accepted at thousands of stations across the EU, the UK and often North Africa or Eastern Europe. Acceptance may run through a negotiated partner network or through a payment scheme such as Visa. Either way, drivers refuel in five countries on one card without rejected transactions.


Second, **consolidated multi-currency invoicing** . Instead of a separate invoice per country, finance receives a single statement itemised by country, currency, supplier and VAT line, ready for accounting software or a VAT-reclaim agent.


Third, **integration of ancillary services** : motorway tolls, vignettes, truck-tolls, EV charging, parking and diesel exhaust fluid. The deeper the integration, the fewer side accounts finance has to chase.


## Why Fleets Switch from a Domestic Fuel Card


Three operational pains push fleets to upgrade.


**The card is declined at the border.** A driver who has used the same domestic card for years hits a French autoroute station or a Spanish forecourt where the card is not accepted, pays personally, and creates a manual expense claim that finance reconciles two weeks later.


**VAT recovery is impossible without help.** Fuel bought in another EU country is recoverable under the 13th Directive and the EU VAT-refund procedure, but only with clean paperwork. Receipts in three languages, three VAT rates and three tax-authority formats rarely meet the bar. Many fleets simply absorb 19 to 27 percent of foreign-fuel cost as a loss.


**Tolls and vignettes live outside the fuel invoice.** Drivers buy vignettes at petrol stations, pay tolls in cash or on personal cards, and add motorway charges through unfamiliar OBUs. Each one is a separate receipt, a separate VAT treatment and a separate place fraud can hide.


An international fuel card collapses all three problems onto one account, one card and one monthly statement.


## How to Evaluate an International Fuel Card in 2026


Every issuer claims European coverage, VAT support and EV charging. The differences only show up when you test the same nine dimensions across your shortlist. Ask for each answer in writing, and ask for it against your own corridors rather than the map on the website.


### 1. Genuine Multi-Country Acceptance


Country counts are the least useful number in this market. A card can list a country on the strength of a few partner sites on one motorway and present it exactly like its home market. What matters is density along the roads your drivers actually use, and what happens when they divert. Take your top ten corridors, list the stations drivers use today, and ask the issuer to confirm acceptance station by station. A network that thins out ten kilometres past the border is a network that will generate personal expense claims.


### 2. Network Acceptance or Payment-Scheme Acceptance


This is the structural difference between the two models. **Network-based** cards are accepted where the issuer has signed a partner agreement, which is why coverage is deep in some countries and thin in others, and why the acceptance map changes when a partnership ends. **Payment-scheme-based** cards run on a card network such as Visa, so acceptance follows the scheme rather than a negotiated list — anywhere the scheme is taken, the card works. Network cards can negotiate site-level discounts and truck-specific facilities; scheme cards trade those for breadth and predictability. Decide which you are buying before you compare prices, because the two models are not priced the same way.


### 3. Cross-Border VAT Recovery and Who Files


Two separate questions hide inside "VAT support". The first is whether the invoice is reclaim-grade: supplier VAT number, date, station, fuel type, volume, net, VAT rate and gross, broken out per country. The second is who actually files. Some issuers run the reclaim for you as a service and take a percentage of what they recover; some hand you a structured file to give to a reclaim agent; some do neither and leave your finance team with a PDF. Establish which of the three you are getting, what it costs, and how long refunds take to land.


### 4. Toll and Vignette Coverage — and Whether You Need a Box


Ask whether tolls arrive on the same invoice as fuel, and whether reaching that point requires separate hardware. For HGVs, most truck-toll regimes need an on-board unit, so the real questions are which countries a single unit covers, who supplies and fits it, what it costs monthly, and what happens if it fails mid-route. For light vehicles, a card that pays at the booth directly often removes the hardware question entirely. Vignettes are worth checking separately, because plenty of cards cover tolls but still leave drivers buying vignettes in cash.


### 5. EV Charging Roaming Across Countries


Treat charging coverage as a distinct network from the fuel network, because it usually is. Ask how many charge points are reachable, in how many countries, and whether roaming works with the same card or requires a second card and app. Check how a driver starts a session when the app fails, whether charging appears on the same invoice with the correct VAT treatment, and whether home charging for company vehicles can be reimbursed through the same account.


### 6. Consolidated Versus Per-Country Invoicing


A card that produces one invoice per country per month has moved the admin, not removed it. Ask for a sample invoice covering at least three countries. Confirm you can get a single statement per legal entity, itemised by country, currency, supplier and VAT line, and that it exports cleanly into your accounting system — Xero, QuickBooks or Sage — without manual re-keying. Check how cost centres, vehicles and drivers are represented, because that determines whether finance can allocate spend without a spreadsheet.


### 7. Currency Handling


Cross-border fleets pay in several currencies, and the FX treatment is often where quiet cost sits. Ask which currencies you can be billed in, what rate is applied, when it is fixed, and whether an FX markup is added on top of it. A card with no FX markup and a transparent rate is easier to budget against than one with a low headline fee and a spread you cannot see.


### 8. Deposits and Credit Terms


Traditional international cards frequently ask for a refundable deposit, a bank guarantee or a personal credit check before they will issue, and may impose minimum monthly volumes. Establish upfront what is required, what it ties up in working capital, and whether terms are prepaid or postpaid. With Rally, prepaid has no refundable security deposit or personal credit check, but business and representative verification still applies. Postpaid terms require separate approval and may involve credit or security requirements.


### 9. Driver Support in Local Languages


A declined card at 2am in a country whose language your driver does not speak is an operational failure, not a support ticket. Ask which languages support is offered in, what the hours are, whether drivers can reach support directly or only through the fleet manager, and how a card is unblocked out of hours. Ask the same about the driver interface — a card whose app is only in English will be used badly by a multinational driver pool.


Use this as the scoring sheet for your shortlist:


Dimension What to ask for Red flag


Acceptance Station-level confirmation on your top 10 corridors Only a country count is offered


Acceptance model Whether it is partner-network or payment-scheme based The answer is vague


VAT recovery Sample reclaim-grade invoice and who files A PDF statement with no VAT breakdown


Tolls and vignettes Countries per OBU, hardware cost, vignette handling Tolls billed separately from fuel


EV charging Countries, roaming, invoice and VAT treatment Charging needs a second card and app


Invoicing One statement per entity, clean accounting export One invoice per country


Currency Billing currencies, FX rate and any markup Rate and markup not disclosed


Deposits and terms Deposit, guarantee, credit check, minimum volume Terms only revealed after a credit check


Driver support Languages, hours, out-of-hours unblocking English-only, office hours

## How Cross-Border VAT Recovery Actually Works


For most European fleets, VAT recovery is where international fuel cards earn their keep. This is a high-level overview, not legal advice — every country has its own rules and a tax advisor should validate the workflow before you rely on it.


When a business pays VAT on fuel in an EU member state where it is not established, the recovery route is the **EU VAT-refund procedure** (the 8th Directive) for businesses established elsewhere in the EU, and the **13th Directive procedure** for non-EU established businesses, such as UK fleets after Brexit. Both rely on the same building blocks: a valid VAT invoice with a clean breakdown by country and rate, and a structured submission through the home country's tax portal (HMRC, AEAT, BZSt).


Manual recovery from paper receipts is slow and expensive. It is not uncommon for fleets to spend €40 to €120 in admin to recover €100 in VAT, which pushes many finance teams to skip recovery altogether.


An international fuel card fixes the upstream problem. The issuer produces a single VAT-ready invoice per country with supplier VAT number, date, station, fuel type, volume, net, VAT rate and gross — everything a reclaim agent needs.


That structured data can be exported directly into your[accounting system](https://www.getrally.com/accounting) or handed to a specialist reclaim agent. Reclaim agents typically charge 5 to 12 percent of recovered VAT, which is far cheaper than running the workflow internally. The result is an effective fuel cost reduction of several percentage points across the fleet — often more meaningful than the headline pence-per-litre discount.


The point to test in a sales conversation is which part of that chain the issuer owns. Producing the invoice, exporting the file and filing the claim are three different commitments, and only the third removes the work from your finance team.


## Tolls, Vignettes, and Mautboxes — One Card or Two?


European tolling is a patchwork the EU's EETS project is slowly unifying but has not yet replaced. The 2026 state of play:


- **France.** A-roads run on dedicated truck-toll tags for HGVs and electronic tags for light vehicles; light tolls can be paid card-by-card at the booth.
- **Italy.** A single national electronic-toll scheme dominates, and multi-country cards integrate with it for HGVs.
- **Spain.** Electronic tags are required for many motorways and are supported by most international cards.
- **Portugal.** A national electronic-toll scheme, supported by most international fuel cards.
- **Germany.** LKW-Maut applies to qualifying goods vehicles and vehicle combinations and runs on Toll Collect OBUs or EETS-compliant alternatives. Our[2026 LKW-Maut refund and toll-management guide](https://www.getrally.com/blog/germany-lkw-maut-refund-for-fleets) covers current thresholds, eligibility, applications, and reconciliation.
- **Switzerland and Austria.** Vignettes for light vehicles plus separate HGV regimes, charged per kilometre and weight.
- **Slovenia, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia.** Each has its own vignette or e-toll regime, handled via dedicated OBUs.


The practical rule: for pure HGV operations, a card paired with a real EETS on-board unit is still the right answer, and the criterion that matters is how many of your countries one unit covers. For vans, service vehicles and lighter mixed fleets, a Visa-backed card pays light-vehicle tolls directly at the booth, consolidates them with fuel and EV charging on one invoice, and avoids the cost of a dedicated OBU.


## EV Charging Across Borders


EV charging is where the international fuel-card market is changing fastest. The historical model — a closed-loop EV card from a single charge point operator — works in the home country but roams poorly across borders. Drivers end up carrying three or four cards and switching apps for each network.


The fuel-card incumbents have responded with roaming products of their own. These are real and useful, but the partner network behind them is thinner than the fuel network and coverage drops outside the issuer's home market. Test it the same way you test fuel acceptance: pick the corridors your electric vehicles actually run, and check charge point availability on those roads rather than the national total.


A modern multi-country[EV charging card for fleets](https://www.getrally.com/ev-charging) like Rally Charge takes a different path: it aggregates roaming partners under a single account, so drivers can start any compatible charger across 20+ countries from one card, fob or WhatsApp message. For mixed van and service-vehicle fleets that electrify faster than long-haul HGVs, this is increasingly the deciding feature. Long-haul operators with HGV-specific charging needs (megawatt charging, dedicated truck stops) will need to follow the truck-charging buildout closely over the next two to three years.


## Choosing the Right Card for Your Fleet


The right international fuel card is the one that maps to your routes, fleet composition, payment terms and admin tolerance. A simple scoring framework cuts through the marketing.


1. **Routes.** List your top 10 corridors and the stations drivers actually use. Score each card on real-world acceptance along those corridors, not advertised country counts.
2. **Pricing.** Pump price plus a flat fee is predictable. Partner pricing plus a service fee can deliver volume rebates at scale but adds variability, and the two models cannot be compared on headline fee alone.
3. **VAT and admin.** If you drive in three or more EU countries, integrated VAT-recovery or VAT-ready invoicing is worth real money. Score cards on the invoice file, not the brochure.
4. **Tolls.** For HGV-heavy fleets, a dedicated EETS OBU is non-negotiable. For light vehicles, a Visa-backed card usually covers tolls without extra hardware.
5. **EV.** If more than 10 percent of your fleet is electric, treat EV-charging coverage as a hard requirement.
6. **Onboarding.** Deposits, credit checks and minimum-volume commitments are still common with traditional providers, and they tie up working capital before you have refuelled once.


Be honest about when a closed-loop card is still the right answer. Deep, truck-only HGV operations with mature LKW-Maut needs and large foreign-VAT volumes are still well-served by a traditional partner-network card with a full toll and reclaim back office. For mixed van, service-vehicle and lighter cross-border fleets that also need EV charging and clean accounting data, a Visa-backed card like Rally usually pays for itself in admin time alone.
